notes.meaning: Jesus and His followers traveled to Cana in Galilee to attend a wedding feast. Jesus' mother Mary was already there, likely helping because the family were relatives or close friends. Joseph is not mentioned, which suggests he had died before this time.

Jesus and His disciples—His group of followers—were invited to the celebration. By coming to the feast, Jesus showed that marriage is honorable and blessed by God. He showed that He takes joy in ordinary human life and wants to be part of our families.

The wedding feast ran out of wine, which would cause great shame and embarrassment for the bridegroom and his family. Mary noticed the shortage and told Jesus about it. She trusted His kindness and looked to Him to help solve the problem.

Jesus answered Mary using the title 'Woman,' which was a polite and respectful term in His language. He gently explained that His miraculous power belonged to God's plan, not to family control. His appointed time to openly reveal His full glory had not yet arrived.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholics believe Jesus addressed Mary as 'woman' to present her as the New Eve promised in Genesis, whose intercession flows from His coming sacrifice.

notes.meaning: Mary accepted Jesus' gentle correction with quiet faith. She turned the servants toward Jesus and told them to obey whatever He said. Her words show that true faith looks to Christ alone and follows His commands.

Six large stone jars stood ready for the Jewish rules of purification, which were ceremonial washings before meals. Each jar held twenty to thirty gallons, so together they could hold a huge quantity of water. Stone containers were preferred because they did not easily become ritually unclean.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholics often view the water of ceremonial purification as a symbol of the Old Covenant that Jesus transforms into the wine of the New Covenant.

notes.meaning: Jesus instructed the servants to fill the stone jars completely with water. The servants followed His directions and filled each jar to the very top. This detail proved that nothing else had been added to the jars to fake a miracle.

Jesus told the servants to dip some of the liquid out and bring it to the director of the feast. It took faith for the servants to take what had just been water to the chief official. Jesus did not use rituals or special words, but simply willed the miracle to happen.

The feast master tasted the water and found that it was now rich wine. He had no idea where the new drink came from, but the servants who drew it knew a miracle had taken place. His unbiased reaction confirmed that the change was real and genuine.

The feast master explained that hosts usually offer their finest wine first, switching to cheaper wine later in the party. He was amazed that the bridegroom had kept the best wine for the end of the celebration. In a spiritual sense, this shows how God saves His greatest blessings for those who follow Christ.

differ.view: Many evangelicals believe Jesus made real, fermented wine, and that the Bible allows moderate drinking while forbidding drunkenness.
Some evangelicals believe Jesus made unfermented grape juice or completely non-alcoholic wine, teaching that Christians should practice total abstinence from alcohol.

notes.meaning: This miracle was the first public sign Jesus gave to show His divine power. Through it He revealed His glory as the Son of God, showing His kindness and authority over nature. The disciples who witnessed this miracle found their early faith in Him greatly deepened.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholics emphasize that Jesus worked this first miracle in response to Mary's request, showing her powerful role as an intercessor for believers.

notes.meaning: Jesus traveled to the lakeside town of Capernaum with His family and disciples for a short rest. Capernaum would soon become the central base for His ministry in Galilee. At this early point, His relatives and followers were still traveling peacefully together.

differ.view: Many evangelicals hold that these brothers were younger biological children born to Mary and Joseph after Jesus.
Some in the Reformed tradition follow early reformers in holding that 'brothers' in Scripture can refer to cousins or close relatives.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholics teach that Mary remained a virgin her whole life, so these 'brothers' were cousins or other near kinsmen rather than Mary's children.

notes.meaning: The Passover was the annual festival celebrating how God freed Israel from slavery in Egypt. Jesus traveled up to Jerusalem to observe this feast in faithful obedience to God's law. His trip also allowed Him to preach to the great crowds gathering in the holy city.

Inside the temple courtyards, Jesus found people running a busy animal market and foreign money exchange. These traders were set up in the Court of the Gentiles, the only place where non-Jewish people could pray. Corrupt temple leaders allowed this business so they could make personal profits.

Jesus braided small ropes into a whip and drove the merchants and livestock out of the temple grounds. He dumped out the money changers' coins and flipped over their trading tables. He showed divine authority against those using holy worship for greedy gain.

Jesus ordered the dove sellers to pack up their cages and leave the temple immediately. He called the temple 'My Father's house,' declaring His unique identity as the Son of God. His Father's house was meant for quiet prayer, not for noisy buying and selling.

Watching Jesus cleanse the courts, His disciples were reminded of Psalm 69:9. That psalm spoke of an intense, burning love for God's holy dwelling that completely takes over a person's life. They saw that Jesus was driven by deep devotion to His Father's honor.

The Jewish authorities confronted Jesus after He drove out the traders. Instead of admitting the temple had been dishonored, they demanded a miraculous sign to prove He had the right to make changes. They refused to accept His authority unless He performed a wonder on the spot.

Jesus gave the leaders a mysterious sign pointing forward to His death and resurrection—His rising back to life. He told them that if they destroyed this temple, He would raise it up in three days. By this He meant that their hatred would kill Him, but He would rise by divine power.

The leaders thought Jesus was talking about the physical temple building in Jerusalem. King Herod had begun rebuilding and expanding that magnificent stone complex forty-six years earlier, and work was still ongoing. To them, claiming to rebuild it in three days sounded foolish and impossible.

John explains that Jesus was using the word 'temple' as a figure of speech for His own physical body. The earthly temple was only a shadow of the true place where God lived among men. In Jesus Christ, the full presence and glory of God dwelt in human flesh.

The disciples did not fully grasp what Jesus meant until after He rose from the grave. Once He was raised, the Holy Spirit brought these words back to their minds. Seeing the prophecy fulfilled gave them stronger trust in both the Old Testament Scriptures and Jesus' own promises.

During the festival week in Jerusalem, many people watched Jesus do miracles and said they believed in Him. They recognized that He had extraordinary power from God. However, much of this belief was shallow, drawn to the excitement of wonders rather than a true change of heart.

Jesus did not put His trust in these crowd members or rely on their enthusiastic praise. He knew human hearts and understood that crowd approval can vanish very quickly. He walked with wisdom, knowing who was sincere and who was unsteady.

Jesus did not need reports or advice from anyone about what people were like inside. As the eternal Son of God, He sees every hidden thought, secret motive, and human flaw. He is the divine searcher of hearts who knows us better than we know ourselves.
